subtopic_detail: Routine antenatal anti-D prophylaxis dosing and timing in an unsensitised RhD negative primigravida
stem:
You are the general practitioner obstetric shared care doctor reviewing a 29 year old primigravid woman at 27 plus 5 weeks. She is RhD negative on her booking group and antibody screen with no anti-D or other red cell antibodies detected. Her partner is RhD positive. Booking bloods otherwise showed haemoglobin 122 g/L, ferritin 42 microgram/L and normal glucose challenge test. She has had no antenatal bleeding, no invasive procedures and no abdominal trauma.

At today's visit she is well, blood pressure 108/68 mmHg, symphysis fundal height 27 cm and fetal heart rate 148 per minute. Cell free foetal DNA to determine foetal RhD group has not been performed at her clinic and is not routinely funded in her state. She has no known allergies. Her next scheduled antenatal visit is at 32 weeks.

data_table.Vital signs: Heart rate 82 /min, blood pressure 108/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degC
data_table.Booking bloods: Group O RhD negative, no red cell antibodies, haemoglobin 122 g/L, ferritin 42 microgram/L
data_table.Obstetric: 27+5 weeks primigravida, no bleeding, no trauma, no invasive procedures
data_table.Foetal: Symphysis fundal height 27 cm, fetal heart 148 /min

lead_in: What is the most appropriate anti-D regimen?

options.text: Give one dose of anti-D 625 IU intramuscularly today at 28 weeks and repeat a second dose of anti-D 625 IU intramuscularly at 34 weeks after a further antibody screen has been performed
options.rationale: The AU National Blood Authority regimen for RhD negative pregnant women is 625 IU intramuscularly at 28 weeks and again at 34 weeks with a preceding antibody screen at each dose. (Source: NBA: Anti-D in Pregnancy)

options.text: Give a single 1500 IU intramuscular anti-D dose today and no further doses until after delivery when a Kleihauer test is performed to determine the need for any supplementary doses in the postnatal period
options.rationale: AU uses split 625 IU regimen at 28 and 34 weeks; a single 1500 IU dose is a UK schedule and is not the funded AU option under the National Blood Authority. (Source: NBA: Anti-D in Pregnancy)

options.text: Defer anti-D until 34 weeks and give a single 625 IU intramuscular dose at that visit only because the earlier 28 week dose is no longer required in current Australian antenatal prophylaxis practice today
options.rationale: The 28 week dose is a core part of the AU two dose regimen; deferring loses first trimester and second trimester silent sensitisation coverage. (Source: NBA: Anti-D in Pregnancy)

options.text: Defer any anti-D until foetal RhD group is confirmed by cell free foetal DNA and only give anti-D if the foetal RhD group returns as RhD positive on the non invasive prenatal test result today
options.rationale: Non invasive foetal RhD typing is available but is not universally funded and is not required to proceed with routine 28 week prophylaxis under AU guidance. (Source: NBA: Anti-D in Pregnancy)

options.text: Perform an antibody screen today, defer anti-D and reassess in 2 weeks with a repeat antibody screen to look for the appearance of anti-D before administering any prophylactic dose in this pregnancy
options.rationale: Antibody screening is performed before each anti-D dose but the 28 week dose itself should not be delayed once the screen is negative. (Source: NBA: Anti-D in Pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Anti-D prophylaxis prevents alloimmunisation in RhD negative women carrying an RhD positive foetus. In Australia the National Blood Authority funds a two dose antenatal regimen of 625 IU intramuscularly at 28 and 34 weeks, each preceded by an antibody screen. Additional doses are given for sensitising events including antepartum haemorrhage, external cephalic version, invasive procedures (chorionic villus sampling, amniocentesis), abdominal trauma and after delivery of a confirmed RhD positive baby (with a Kleihauer test to guide additional doses if a large foeto-maternal haemorrhage is suspected). Non invasive foetal RhD typing by cell free DNA is available in some jurisdictions but is not required for routine prophylaxis.
key_points: AU regimen: anti-D 625 IU intramuscular at 28 weeks and 34 weeks, each after an antibody screen.
Additional doses for sensitising events (bleeding, ECV, trauma, invasive procedures, delivery).
Kleihauer test after delivery guides additional postnatal dose for large foeto-maternal haemorrhage.
explanation.pearls: The AU National Blood Authority anti-D antenatal schedule is two 625 IU intramuscular doses (28 and 34 weeks), each preceded by an antibody screen; sensitising events (bleeding, ECV, invasive procedures) require an additional dose.

subtopic_detail: First line pharmacological therapy for uterine atony postpartum haemorrhage of 800 mL at 10 minutes after normal vaginal delivery
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in the birth suite. A 34 year old parous woman has just delivered a healthy 3.8 kg baby by normal vaginal delivery after a 6 hour labour. Third stage was actively managed with intramuscular oxytocin 10 IU at delivery of the anterior shoulder. Ten minutes after delivery the estimated blood loss is 800 mL with ongoing brisk vaginal bleeding.

The midwife reports the uterus is soft and poorly contracted on palpation. Blood pressure is 108/62 mmHg (baseline 118/72), heart rate 108 per minute, oxygen saturation 99 percent on room air. Bimanual examination shows the placenta appears complete on inspection, no cervical, vaginal or perineal lacerations visible on speculum, and no clots retained in the vagina. She had a normal antenatal course with no known bleeding disorder. She has an 18 gauge peripheral intravenous cannula and full blood count and coagulation samples are being collected.

data_table.Vital signs: Heart rate 108 /min, blood pressure 108/62 mmHg (baseline 118/72), respiratory rate 20 /min, SpO2 99% on room air
data_table.Uterine: Uterus soft and poorly contracted, ongoing brisk vaginal bleeding
data_table.Assessment: Placenta complete on inspection, no visible cervical/vaginal/perineal lacerations, no retained clots
data_table.Loss: Estimated blood loss 800 mL at 10 minutes postpartum

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial pharmacological step?

options.text: Give intramuscular carboprost 250 microgram now and prepare to repeat every 15 minutes to a maximum of eight doses if bleeding continues without additional uterotonic therapy in the interim
options.rationale: Carboprost is a second line uterotonic used after oxytocin and ergometrine have failed; it is contraindicated in asthma. (Source: RANZCOG: Postpartum Haemorrhage)

options.text: Start an intravenous oxytocin infusion 40 IU in 1000 mL Hartmann's solution at 250 mL per hour with immediate uterine massage while preparing intramuscular ergometrine 250 microgram as second line
options.rationale: First line for uterine atony after active management is intravenous oxytocin infusion plus fundal massage; ergometrine is second line unless contraindicated by hypertension. (Source: RANZCOG: Postpartum Haemorrhage)

options.text: Give intravenous tranexamic acid 1 g bolus over 10 minutes now and defer any further uterotonic administration until the tranexamic acid effect has been assessed at 30 minutes after the initial dose
options.rationale: Tranexamic acid is an important adjunct within 3 hours but does not replace uterotonics as first line for atonic postpartum haemorrhage. (Source: RANZCOG: Postpartum Haemorrhage)

options.text: Give sublingual misoprostol 800 microgram immediately as the first line pharmacological agent for atonic postpartum haemorrhage and reassess bleeding at 20 minutes after the sublingual dose has been given
options.rationale: Misoprostol is a resource limited or adjunct option; intravenous oxytocin is first line where available. (Source: RANZCOG: Postpartum Haemorrhage)

options.text: Insert an intrauterine balloon tamponade device immediately as the first line intervention for atonic postpartum haemorrhage before any additional pharmacological uterotonic therapy is trialled or administered
options.rationale: Balloon tamponade is used after failure of pharmacological measures (oxytocin, ergometrine, carboprost) or when medical therapy is contraindicated. (Source: RANZCOG: Postpartum Haemorrhage)

explanation.summary: Uterine atony causes around 70 percent of primary postpartum haemorrhage. First line management is a coordinated response with fundal massage, an intravenous oxytocin infusion (40 IU in 1000 mL crystalloid at 250 mL per hour), simultaneous exclusion of retained products and lacerations, and prompt escalation. Ergometrine 250 microgram intramuscular is second line unless the woman is hypertensive. Carboprost 250 microgram intramuscular is third line and is contraindicated in asthma. Tranexamic acid 1 g intravenous within 3 hours reduces mortality from postpartum haemorrhage. Balloon tamponade, uterine artery embolisation, B-Lynch suture and hysterectomy follow if pharmacological measures fail. Call for senior obstetric, anaesthetic and haematology support early.
key_points: First line for atony: intravenous oxytocin infusion (40 IU/L at 250 mL/h) plus fundal massage.
Second line: ergometrine 250 microgram intramuscular (avoid in hypertension).
Tranexamic acid 1 g intravenous within 3 hours reduces mortality; not a first line uterotonic.
explanation.pearls: In postpartum haemorrhage from uterine atony, start an intravenous oxytocin infusion 40 IU in 1 L at 250 mL/h plus fundal massage first; escalate to intramuscular ergometrine 250 microgram if bleeding continues (avoid if hypertensive).

subtopic_detail: Expectant management timing decision in confirmed preterm prelabour rupture of membranes at 33 plus 2 weeks without chorioamnionitis
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 29 year old parous woman at 33 plus 2 weeks with confirmed preterm prelabour rupture of membranes 6 hours ago. The diagnosis was made on speculum showing pooling of clear liquor and positive placental alpha microglobulin 1 test. There are no contractions. Cardiotocograph is reactive with no decelerations.

Maternal temperature is 36.8 degC, heart rate 84 per minute, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, C reactive protein 8 mg/L (below 5) and white cell count 9.6 x10^9/L. Group B Streptococcus swab at 34 weeks was not performed as this rupture is her first presentation. She has no allergies. She has already received the first dose of intramuscular betamethasone 11.4 mg 4 hours ago and the second dose is scheduled at 24 hours. The maternity unit has neonatal intensive care level 3 on site with respiratory support and ventilation available for babies born from 32 weeks.

data_table.Vital signs: Heart rate 84 /min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degC
data_table.Bloods: C reactive protein 8 mg/L (below 5), white cell count 9.6 x10^9/L
data_table.Foetal: Cardiotocograph reactive, no decelerations, no contractions
data_table.Rupture: Confirmed clear liquor on speculum, positive placental alpha microglobulin 1 test 6 hours ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Induce labour with vaginal prostaglandin E2 today because ongoing expectant management beyond 32 weeks confers no additional foetal benefit and increases the risk of maternal and neonatal chorioamnionitis significantly
options.rationale: The PPROMT trial and RANZCOG guidance support expectant management to 37 weeks in the absence of infection or foetal compromise; immediate induction at 33 plus 2 without infection is not first line. (Source: RANZCOG: Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes

options.text: Perform an emergency caesarean section this evening once the second corticosteroid dose is complete because vaginal birth after preterm prelabour rupture of membranes carries an unacceptable rate of neonatal sepsis at this gestation
options.rationale: Route of delivery is decided by usual obstetric indications; caesarean is not the default for preterm prelabour rupture of membranes and does not reduce sepsis. (Source: RANZCOG: Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes

options.text: Admit for expectant management with intravenous cefazolin then oral erythromycin per protocol, complete the corticosteroid course, monitor for infection and plan delivery at 37 weeks in the absence of chorioamnionitis
options.rationale: AU practice for preterm prelabour rupture of membranes without infection or foetal compromise is expectant management to 37 weeks with intravenous then oral antibiotics, corticosteroids, and daily surveillance for chorioamnionitis. (Source: RANZCOG: Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes

options.text: Commence intramuscular magnesium sulfate 4 g load and 1 g per hour infusion for foetal neuroprotection now and continue for the full 24 hour infusion prior to any subsequent delivery decision at this gestation
options.rationale: Magnesium sulfate for foetal neuroprotection is given for imminent preterm delivery below 30 weeks; at 33 plus 2 weeks with no labour it is not indicated. (Source: RANZCOG: Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes

options.text: Give tocolysis with intravenous atosiban 6.75 mg bolus and infusion for 48 hours to prolong the pregnancy until the corticosteroid course completes and neonatal intensive care support is optimised
options.rationale: Tocolysis is not indicated in preterm prelabour rupture of membranes without active labour and may mask infection; her cardiotocograph shows no contractions. (Source: RANZCOG: Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes

explanation.summary: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes affects around 3 percent of pregnancies. In Australia, RANZCOG guidance (informed by the PPROMT trial) supports expectant management until 37 weeks in the absence of infection, placental abruption or foetal compromise, because immediate delivery at 34 to 36 weeks increases neonatal respiratory distress without reducing neonatal sepsis. Management includes antenatal corticosteroids (before 34 weeks), latency antibiotics (usually intravenous benzylpenicillin then oral erythromycin per unit protocol), daily maternal observations and foetal surveillance, and Group B Streptococcus prophylaxis in labour. Magnesium sulfate for foetal neuroprotection is reserved for imminent birth below 30 weeks. Tocolysis is not indicated in the absence of active labour and may mask evolving chorioamnionitis.
key_points: Expectant management to 37 weeks is the AU default in preterm prelabour rupture of membranes without infection or foetal compromise.
Corticosteroids for foetal lung maturity if under 34 weeks; latency antibiotics per protocol.
Magnesium sulfate neuroprotection only for imminent birth below 30 weeks; no tocolysis in preterm prelabour rupture of membranes without labour.
explanation.pearls: Expectant management to 37 weeks (with corticosteroids under 34 weeks and latency antibiotics) is the RANZCOG default for preterm prelabour rupture of membranes in the absence of infection or foetal compromise, following PPROMT trial evidence.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes

subtopic_detail: Suspected complete hydatidiform mole with markedly elevated beta hCG, hyperemesis and classic ultrasound features at 9 weeks
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar reviewing a 27 year old primigravid woman at 9 plus 2 weeks by dates with severe hyperemesis, dark brown vaginal discharge for 3 days and passage of a grape like fragment yesterday. She has no significant medical history. She is on oral pyridoxine and doxylamine for nausea with limited benefit.

On examination she is dehydrated, pulse 108 per minute, blood pressure 108/68 mmHg, temperature 36.8 degC. Uterus is palpable 4 cm above the pubic symphysis (larger than dates). Serum beta hCG is 380000 IU/L (expected 20000 to 120000 at 9 weeks). Transvaginal ultrasound shows an enlarged uterus, no foetal parts, an echogenic intrauterine mass with numerous small anechoic spaces described by the radiologist as a snowstorm pattern, no obvious foetal heart activity and bilateral 5 cm theca lutein cysts. Thyroid stimulating hormone is 0.02 mIU/L (0.4 to 4.0) and free thyroxine is 24 pmol/L (10 to 20). Full blood count and coagulation are within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: Heart rate 108 /min, blood pressure 108/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degC
data_table.Ultrasound: Enlarged uterus, no foetal parts, echogenic intrauterine mass with numerous small anechoic spaces (snowstorm), no foetal cardiac activity, bilateral 5 cm theca lutein cysts
data_table.Biochemistry: Beta hCG 380000 IU/L (expected 20000-120000), TSH 0.02 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), free T4 24 pmol/L (10-20)
data_table.Clinical: Severe hyperemesis, dark brown discharge 3 days, passage of grape-like fragment, uterus larger than dates

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Prescribe methotrexate 50 mg per m2 intramuscular single dose today for medical management of a presumed ectopic pregnancy or non viable intrauterine pregnancy before considering any surgical intervention or referral
options.rationale: Molar pregnancy is not an ectopic pregnancy; methotrexate is not the initial treatment of a hydatidiform mole (suction curettage is) and may be used later for gestational trophoblastic neoplasia. (Source: RANZCOG: Gestational Trophoblastic Disease)

options.text: Arrange elective surgical evacuation by dilatation and sharp curettage in 2 weeks time as an outpatient day surgery procedure with a general practitioner review at 6 weeks after the procedure has been completed
options.rationale: Sharp curettage risks uterine perforation in molar pregnancy; suction curettage is the preferred technique and evacuation should not be delayed 2 weeks given ongoing bleeding and hyperthyroid symptoms. (Source: RANZCOG: Gestational Trophoblastic Disease)

options.text: Give intravenous oxytocin infusion 40 IU in 1000 mL Hartmann's solution to induce expulsion of the molar tissue without any subsequent surgical intervention or gynaecology admission for further inpatient care
options.rationale: Oxytocin infusion pre-evacuation increases the risk of embolic spread of trophoblastic tissue; suction evacuation is definitive and oxytocin is used cautiously after cervical dilatation. (Source: RANZCOG: Gestational Trophoblastic Disease)

options.text: Admit today for suction curettage of the uterine contents under general anaesthesia with histopathology, group and hold, and enrol in the state gestational trophoblastic disease registry for serial hCG surveillance
options.rationale: Suction curettage under general anaesthesia with histopathology is the AU first line for complete hydatidiform mole; enrolment in the state registry ensures serial beta hCG surveillance for gestational trophoblastic neoplasia. (Source: RANZCOG: Gestational Trophoblastic Disease)

options.text: Perform total abdominal hysterectomy urgently today for definitive management of the suspected molar pregnancy and to prevent the development of subsequent gestational trophoblastic neoplasia in this patient population
options.rationale: Hysterectomy is reserved for women who have completed childbearing or for chemoresistant disease; it is not the first line for a molar pregnancy in a 27 year old primigravida. (Source: RANZCOG: Gestational Trophoblastic Disease)

explanation.summary: Complete hydatidiform mole classically presents with vaginal bleeding, uterus larger than dates, markedly elevated beta hCG, hyperemesis and biochemical hyperthyroidism from beta hCG cross reactivity with the thyroid stimulating hormone receptor. Ultrasound shows a snowstorm or cluster of grapes appearance with theca lutein cysts. First line management is suction curettage under general anaesthesia with histopathology and group and hold; oxytocin is used cautiously after cervical dilatation to reduce blood loss without precipitating trophoblastic embolisation. After evacuation, enrolment in the state gestational trophoblastic disease registry for serial beta hCG measurement (weekly until normal for 3 weeks, then monthly for 6 months) allows early detection of gestational trophoblastic neoplasia. Contraception is required during surveillance; the intrauterine device is avoided until beta hCG normalises.
key_points: Complete hydatidiform mole: uterus larger than dates, beta hCG very elevated, snowstorm ultrasound, biochemical hyperthyroidism.
First line: suction curettage under general anaesthesia with histopathology.
Enrol in state gestational trophoblastic disease registry for serial beta hCG surveillance.
explanation.pearls: Enrol every complete hydatidiform mole in the state gestational trophoblastic disease registry for serial beta hCG (weekly until normal for 3 weeks then monthly for 6 months); avoid intrauterine device contraception until beta hCG normalises.

subtopic_detail: Antenatal referral and delivery planning for a woman with three prior caesarean sections and a low anterior placenta at 32 weeks with placenta accreta spectrum features on ultrasound
stem:
You are the general practitioner obstetric shared care doctor reviewing a 36 year old woman at 32 weeks in her fourth pregnancy. She has had three previous lower segment caesarean sections and is otherwise well. Her 32 week transvaginal ultrasound performed today shows an anterior placenta praevia (edge covering the internal os) with placental lacunae, loss of the retroplacental hypoechoic zone and bridging vessels between the placenta and the bladder wall. The reporting sonographer flags high suspicion of placenta accreta spectrum.

Her current haemoglobin is 108 g/L, ferritin 22 microgram/L, blood group A RhD positive with no antibodies. Blood pressure is 118/76 mmHg. She has no antepartum bleeding to date, no contractions and a normal cardiotocograph. She lives 45 minutes from the tertiary centre where she previously delivered. She has been given information about the ultrasound findings and asks what happens next.

data_table.Vital signs: Heart rate 82 /min, blood pressure 118/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 /min, SpO2 99% on room air
data_table.Ultrasound: Anterior placenta praevia over internal os, placental lacunae, loss of retroplacental hypoechoic zone, bridging vessels to bladder wall
data_table.Obstetric: G4P3 with three prior caesarean sections, 32 weeks, no bleeding or contractions
data_table.Bloods: Haemoglobin 108 g/L, ferritin 22 microgram/L, group A RhD positive, no antibodies

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue routine general practitioner shared care with a repeat ultrasound at 36 weeks to reassess for resolution of the low placental position and plan delivery in the local community hospital
options.rationale: Placenta accreta spectrum features with three prior caesareans and anterior praevia is high risk; local hospital delivery misses the multidisciplinary team required. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta Accreta Spectrum)

options.text: Admit today for immediate elective lower segment caesarean section under general anaesthesia at 32 weeks to remove the placenta before the risk of massive antepartum haemorrhage increases with advancing gestation
options.rationale: Immediate delivery at 32 weeks incurs preterm neonatal morbidity without benefit in the absence of active bleeding; planned delivery at 34 to 36 weeks after multidisciplinary planning is preferred. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta Accreta Spectrum)

options.text: Perform amniocentesis at 34 weeks to confirm foetal lung maturity and only proceed to delivery once the lecithin to sphingomyelin ratio is confirmed as mature at greater than 2 for the current pregnancy
options.rationale: Amniocentesis for lung maturity is not routinely used in AU; timing is by gestation and clinical status with antenatal corticosteroids where appropriate. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta Accreta Spectrum)

options.text: Refer to a tertiary maternal foetal medicine unit for consideration of elective classical caesarean section with immediate hysterectomy at 39 weeks by the general obstetric team on call
options.rationale: Delivery at 39 weeks is too late (risk of labour or bleeding); planned delivery at 34 to 36 plus 6 by a dedicated placenta accreta spectrum multidisciplinary team is standard. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta Accreta Spectrum)

options.text: Refer to a tertiary placenta accreta spectrum multidisciplinary team for planned caesarean hysterectomy at 34 to 36 plus 6 weeks with antenatal corticosteroids and cell salvage plus massive transfusion protocol readiness
options.rationale: AU RANZCOG standard is referral to a placenta accreta spectrum multidisciplinary team with planned delivery at 34 to 36 plus 6 weeks under antenatal corticosteroids, with cell salvage and massive transfusion protocol ready. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta Accreta Spectrum)

explanation.summary: Placenta accreta spectrum (accreta, increta, percreta) risk rises steeply with the number of previous caesarean sections and coexisting placenta praevia. Antenatal ultrasound features include placental lacunae (Swiss cheese appearance), loss of the retroplacental hypoechoic zone, thinning or interruption of the bladder wall interface and bridging vessels. Magnetic resonance imaging is used adjunctively. Standard Australian management is referral to a tertiary maternal foetal medicine unit with a dedicated placenta accreta spectrum team, antenatal corticosteroids and planned caesarean hysterectomy at 34 to 36 plus 6 weeks (earlier for bleeding or preterm labour). Intraoperative preparation includes cell salvage, massive transfusion protocol readiness, interventional radiology for uterine artery occlusion balloons and multidisciplinary theatre team.
key_points: Placenta accreta spectrum risk rises with number of previous caesarean sections plus placenta praevia.
AU planned delivery at 34 to 36 plus 6 weeks with antenatal corticosteroids in a tertiary centre.
Prepare cell salvage, massive transfusion protocol and interventional radiology support.
explanation.pearls: Placenta accreta spectrum with an anterior praevia over prior caesarean scars is planned for caesarean hysterectomy at 34 to 36 plus 6 weeks in a tertiary centre with cell salvage and massive transfusion protocol activated preoperatively.

subtopic_detail: Recognition and immediate management of amniotic fluid embolism presenting as intrapartum collapse with disseminated intravascular coagulation
stem:
You are the obstetric consultant urgently called to the birth suite where a 33 year old parous woman at 40 weeks has just delivered a live baby by normal vaginal delivery after 30 minutes of second stage. Immediately after delivery she developed sudden onset dyspnoea, agitation and then loss of consciousness with cardiovascular collapse. Blood pressure was unrecordable and heart rate 148 per minute on the pulse oximeter waveform. Cardiopulmonary resuscitation was commenced with return of spontaneous circulation after 3 minutes and she is now intubated and ventilated with a pulse of 128 per minute and blood pressure 78/42 mmHg on adrenaline infusion.

She is oozing brisk fresh red blood from her venepuncture sites and from the vaginal delivery bed. Urgent bloods show haemoglobin 82 g/L, platelets 42 x10^9/L (150 to 400), prothrombin time 26 seconds (11 to 15), activated partial thromboplastin time 68 seconds (25 to 35), fibrinogen 0.8 g/L (2.0 to 4.0), D-dimer above 20 mg/L. Arterial blood gas shows pH 7.14, PaO2 62 mmHg on FiO2 1.0, PaCO2 52 mmHg. There is no evidence of retained products, uterine rupture, cervical laceration or amniotic fluid still leaking. She has no known allergies and no comorbidities.

data_table.Vital signs: Heart rate 128 /min, blood pressure 78/42 mmHg on adrenaline, respiratory rate 16 /min (ventilated), SpO2 88% on FiO2 1.0
data_table.Coagulation: Platelets 42 x10^9/L (150-400), PT 26 s (11-15), APTT 68 s (25-35), fibrinogen 0.8 g/L (2.0-4.0), D-dimer >20 mg/L
data_table.Blood gas: pH 7.14, PaO2 62 mmHg on FiO2 1.0, PaCO2 52 mmHg
data_table.Clinical: Fresh bleeding from venepuncture sites and vaginal bed; no retained products, no uterine rupture on inspection

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Activate the massive transfusion protocol, give fibrinogen concentrate 4 g or cryoprecipitate 10 units and administer packed red cells, fresh frozen plasma and platelets in 1 to 1 to 1 ratio guided by ROTEM
options.rationale: Amniotic fluid embolism causes early consumptive coagulopathy; rapid fibrinogen replacement (aim above 2 g/L) and 1 to 1 to 1 blood product resuscitation guided by ROTEM is the AU obstetric massive haemorrhage standard. (Source: NBA: Patient Blood Management)

options.text: Give intravenous heparin 5000 units bolus and infusion for disseminated intravascular coagulation with active thrombosis before considering any blood component transfusion or reversal of the coagulopathy
options.rationale: Heparin is contraindicated in obstetric disseminated intravascular coagulation with active haemorrhage; the phenotype is consumptive bleeding not thrombosis. (Source: NBA: Patient Blood Management)

options.text: Give intravenous recombinant activated factor VII 90 microgram per kg as first line treatment for the coagulopathy without first replacing fibrinogen or platelets or correcting acidosis prior to administration
options.rationale: Recombinant activated factor VII carries a high thrombotic risk and requires baseline fibrinogen above 1.5 g/L, platelets above 50 and pH above 7.2; it is not first line in amniotic fluid embolism coagulopathy. (Source: NBA: Patient Blood Management)

options.text: Give intravenous tranexamic acid 4 g bolus over 5 minutes as the only initial treatment and defer blood component transfusion until the tranexamic acid has been given time to exert its full anti-fibrinolytic effect
options.rationale: Tranexamic acid 1 g intravenous is an adjunct but does not replace fibrinogen and platelet replacement in fulminant amniotic fluid embolism coagulopathy; the standard dose is 1 g not 4 g bolus. (Source: NBA: Patient Blood Management)

options.text: Give intravenous atropine 1 mg, intravenous ondansetron 8 mg and intravenous ketorolac 30 mg (the A-OK protocol) as monotherapy and defer any blood product transfusion or additional resuscitation until reassessment at 30 minutes
options.rationale: A-OK is an adjunct protocol targeting vasoactive mediators; it does not replace haemorrhage resuscitation with blood products and coagulopathy correction. (Source: NBA: Patient Blood Management)

explanation.summary: Amniotic fluid embolism is a rare (2 to 8 per 100000 deliveries) but catastrophic obstetric emergency presenting with a triad of hypoxia, hypotension and consumptive coagulopathy occurring around labour or in the immediate postpartum period. Diagnosis is clinical and requires exclusion of alternatives (pulmonary embolism, sepsis, anaphylaxis, uterine rupture). Immediate management is high quality cardiopulmonary resuscitation with left uterine displacement (or perimortem caesarean within 4 minutes if arrest before delivery), airway support, vasopressor support (noradrenaline or adrenaline), correction of coagulopathy with early fibrinogen (concentrate or cryoprecipitate) targeting fibrinogen above 2 g/L, and balanced 1 to 1 to 1 blood component resuscitation guided by ROTEM or thromboelastography. Tranexamic acid 1 g is an adjunct. Recombinant activated factor VII is reserved for refractory bleeding after correction of pH, fibrinogen and platelets. Maternal mortality remains around 20 to 40 percent in Australia.
key_points: Amniotic fluid embolism triad: hypoxia, hypotension, consumptive coagulopathy peri-partum.
Early fibrinogen replacement (concentrate or cryoprecipitate) targeting fibrinogen above 2 g/L.
1 to 1 to 1 packed cells to fresh frozen plasma to platelets, guided by ROTEM.
explanation.pearls: In suspected amniotic fluid embolism give fibrinogen concentrate 4 g or 10 units of cryoprecipitate early to target fibrinogen above 2 g/L; recombinant factor VII is reserved for refractory bleeding after fibrinogen, platelets and pH are corrected.

subtopic_detail: First line smoking cessation pharmacotherapy for an adult smoker with well controlled major depression on sertraline
stem:
You are a general practitioner reviewing a 44 year old woman who wishes to stop smoking. She smokes 20 cigarettes per day and has done so for 20 pack years. She has previously stopped for 6 weeks using nicotine patches alone 3 years ago before relapse. She has major depressive disorder in remission on sertraline 100 mg daily for 18 months with no depressive symptoms and no suicidal ideation.

She has no cardiovascular disease, no seizures, normal renal function and no personal or family history of psychosis. Her body mass index is 24 kg per m2 and her blood pressure is 118/76 mmHg. She has a supportive partner and is enrolled in a workplace quit program with weekly counselling. Her Fagerstrom test score is 6, indicating moderate to high nicotine dependence. She reports smoking her first cigarette within 5 minutes of waking.

data_table.Vital signs: Heart rate 76 /min, blood pressure 118/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 /min, SpO2 98% on room air
data_table.Smoking: 20 cigarettes/day, 20 pack-year history, first cigarette within 5 minutes of waking, Fagerstrom 6
data_table.Mental health: Major depressive disorder in remission on sertraline 100 mg daily, no suicidal ideation, no psychosis
data_table.Prior attempts: 6 weeks abstinent on nicotine patches alone 3 years ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Prescribe nicotine patches 21 mg daily alone for 12 weeks as first line pharmacotherapy because varenicline is contraindicated in patients with a diagnosed history of major depressive disorder on antidepressant therapy currently
options.rationale: Varenicline is not contraindicated in stable depression; the EAGLES trial found no increased neuropsychiatric risk in psychiatrically stable patients. Combination NRT (patch plus lozenge) is preferred over patch monotherapy. (Source: eTG: Smoking Cessation)

options.text: Prescribe varenicline 0.5 mg daily for 3 days then 0.5 mg twice daily for 4 days then 1 mg twice daily for 12 weeks with a target quit date 1 week after starting and continue sertraline unchanged
options.rationale: Varenicline is first line for moderate to high dependence smokers and is not contraindicated in stable depression; the EAGLES trial found no increased neuropsychiatric risk versus placebo. (Source: eTG: Smoking Cessation)

options.text: Prescribe bupropion 150 mg once daily for 3 days then 150 mg twice daily for 9 weeks as first line pharmacotherapy plus stop sertraline 2 weeks before starting bupropion to reduce the risk of serotonin syndrome
options.rationale: Bupropion is not first line in a patient with recent depression and it is not necessary to stop sertraline; risk of seizure and serotonin syndrome does not require this pre-treatment washout. (Source: eTG: Smoking Cessation)

options.text: Refer to an inpatient specialist smoking cessation unit for supervised nicotine withdrawal because outpatient pharmacotherapy is unsuitable in patients with prior relapse on nicotine replacement therapy alone at any dose
options.rationale: Inpatient smoking cessation is not standard AU practice; outpatient pharmacotherapy with counselling is first line even with prior relapse. (Source: eTG: Smoking Cessation)

options.text: Prescribe cytisine 1.5 mg titrated over 25 days as first line pharmacotherapy for smoking cessation because it is safer than varenicline in a patient with stable major depressive disorder on antidepressant therapy today
options.rationale: Cytisine is a partial nicotinic agonist supported by evidence but is not first line under current AU guidance; varenicline remains preferred for high dependence smokers where available. (Source: eTG: Smoking Cessation)

explanation.summary: First line pharmacotherapy for adult smoking cessation in Australia is varenicline, combination nicotine replacement therapy (patch plus intermittent lozenge, gum, spray or inhaler) or bupropion; all approximately double sustained quit rates versus placebo. Varenicline (a partial alpha4 beta2 nicotinic acetylcholine receptor agonist) is titrated over 7 days to 1 mg twice daily for 12 weeks with a target quit date 1 to 2 weeks after starting. The EAGLES trial demonstrated no increased risk of significant neuropsychiatric adverse events in psychiatrically stable patients including those with treated depression, removing the earlier boxed warning. Combination nicotine replacement therapy is preferred to monotherapy in moderate to high dependence smokers. Behavioural support (Quitline, workplace programs, general practitioner counselling) doubles cessation rates when combined with pharmacotherapy.
key_points: AU first line: varenicline, combination nicotine replacement therapy, or bupropion.
Varenicline titration: 0.5 mg daily for 3 days, 0.5 mg twice daily for 4 days, then 1 mg twice daily for 12 weeks.
EAGLES trial: no increased neuropsychiatric risk with varenicline in psychiatrically stable patients.
explanation.pearls: Varenicline is not contraindicated in stable depression on antidepressant therapy following the EAGLES trial; titrate over 7 days to 1 mg twice daily with a quit date 1 week after starting for a 12 week course.

subtopic_detail: First line stimulant choice and prescribing pathway for a newly diagnosed adult with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar in a community adult ADHD clinic reviewing a 28 year old man newly diagnosed with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder combined presentation using the DIVA structured interview. Childhood history is consistent with symptoms before age 12 corroborated by his mother. He works as a graphic designer and reports significant impairment in meeting deadlines. He has no history of substance use disorder, no cardiovascular disease, no psychosis and no mania.

Blood pressure is 122/74 mmHg, resting heart rate 74 per minute, body mass index 24 kg per m2 and baseline electrocardiogram shows sinus rhythm with QTc 410 milliseconds. He has no family history of sudden cardiac death or long QT. He is not on any current medication and has no allergies. He lives with his partner, has a driver's licence and does not currently drink alcohol or smoke. He agrees to shared care with his general practitioner in your state where authority prescribing rules apply.

data_table.Vital signs: Heart rate 74 /min, blood pressure 122/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 /min, SpO2 99% on room air
data_table.Cardiac: Electrocardiogram sinus rhythm, QTc 410 milliseconds, no family history of sudden death
data_table.Diagnostic: DIVA structured interview positive for combined presentation, childhood corroboration by mother
data_table.Substance/psychiatric: No substance use disorder, no psychosis, no mania

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Prescribe atomoxetine 40 mg daily titrated to 80 mg daily over 4 weeks as first line and monitor liver function every 3 months for hepatotoxicity because non stimulants are preferred over stimulants in adult ADHD today
options.rationale: Non stimulants (atomoxetine, guanfacine) are second line for adult ADHD in AU; stimulants (methylphenidate or dexamphetamine derivatives) are first line unless contraindicated. (Source: RANZCP: ADHD)

options.text: Prescribe modafinil 200 mg daily as first line pharmacotherapy for adult attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and titrate to 400 mg daily over 2 weeks with weekly clinical review during the initial titration phase
options.rationale: Modafinil is not registered nor first line for adult ADHD in AU; use is off label with limited evidence. (Source: RANZCP: ADHD)

options.text: Prescribe lisdexamfetamine 30 mg once daily in the morning as first line, titrate at 30 mg weekly increments to target response, and review at 4 weeks with blood pressure, heart rate and side effect check
options.rationale: AU first line for adult ADHD is a long acting stimulant (lisdexamfetamine or methylphenidate extended release), starting at 30 mg daily lisdexamfetamine and titrating weekly with cardiovascular monitoring. (Source: RANZCP: ADHD)

options.text: Prescribe bupropion sustained release 150 mg daily titrated to 300 mg daily as first line pharmacotherapy for adult attention deficit hyperactivity disorder to reduce the risk of stimulant misuse in an adult population today
options.rationale: Bupropion has some efficacy but is not first line for adult ADHD in AU; stimulant misuse is not a routine contraindication in a patient without substance use disorder. (Source: RANZCP: ADHD)

options.text: Prescribe risperidone 1 mg at night as first line pharmacotherapy for adult attention deficit hyperactivity disorder to reduce impulsivity and hyperactivity symptoms before considering stimulant medication for cognitive impairment
options.rationale: Antipsychotics are not indicated for adult ADHD and add metabolic and extrapyramidal risk. (Source: RANZCP: ADHD)

explanation.summary: Adult attention deficit hyperactivity disorder in Australia is diagnosed by clinical interview (often using DIVA or CAADID) with corroboration of childhood symptoms before age 12. First line pharmacotherapy is a long acting stimulant, either lisdexamfetamine (30 to 70 mg once daily) or methylphenidate extended release, titrated to symptom control. Baseline assessment includes cardiovascular history, blood pressure, heart rate, personal and family history of sudden death or arrhythmia, and 12 lead electrocardiogram if any red flag. Absolute contraindications include structural cardiac disease, moderate to severe hypertension, hyperthyroidism, phaeochromocytoma and current substance dependence. Non stimulants (atomoxetine, guanfacine) are second line. All states require authority or specialist prescribing for stimulants; shared care with the general practitioner is standard. Cardiovascular monitoring continues 3 to 6 monthly.
key_points: AU first line: long acting stimulant (lisdexamfetamine 30 mg daily or methylphenidate extended release).
Baseline: blood pressure, heart rate, cardiovascular family history; electrocardiogram if red flag.
Non stimulants (atomoxetine, guanfacine) are second line; antipsychotics have no role.
explanation.pearls: Lisdexamfetamine 30 mg daily is the AU first line adult ADHD stimulant when cardiovascular assessment is clear; escalate at 30 mg weekly increments (maximum 70 mg) with blood pressure and heart rate review at 4 weeks.

subtopic_detail: Emergency department management of chronic self-harm in a woman with borderline personality disorder attending after a superficial forearm cut without medical severity
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar reviewing a 26 year old woman with a 5 year diagnosis of borderline personality disorder brought in by her mother after cutting her left forearm at home 2 hours ago following an argument with her partner. She has 12 previous emergency department presentations for similar self injury in the last year. She engages in a dialectical behaviour therapy group weekly and has a case manager.

Examination shows a 6 cm superficial cut on the volar left forearm not extending through the dermis with no active bleeding, no tendon or nerve involvement and normal distal neurovascular examination. Blood pressure is 118/72 mmHg, heart rate 84 per minute, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degC. She denies current suicidal intent but reports urge for further self injury if she goes home in the current state. She rates distress 8 out of 10. She has taken no drugs or alcohol; blood alcohol is 0.00 percent and urine drug screen is negative. Her case manager is contactable and dialectical behaviour therapy team lead is available today.

data_table.Vital signs: Heart rate 84 /min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degC
data_table.Wound: 6 cm superficial cut left volar forearm, no active bleeding, no tendon or nerve involvement, normal distal neurovascular exam
data_table.Toxicology: Blood alcohol 0.00%, urine drug screen negative
data_table.Mental state: Denies suicidal intent, reports urge for further self injury, distress 8/10, engaged with weekly dialectical behaviour therapy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Admit involuntarily to an acute psychiatric unit under the Mental Health Act because of active urge for self injury and recent recurrent presentations that place her at high risk of completed suicide over the next 24 to 48 hours
options.rationale: Involuntary admission for chronic self injury without imminent risk of suicide is contrary to AU guidance; hospitalisation risks iatrogenic harm and regression. (Source: NHMRC: Borderline Personality Disorder Guideline)

options.text: Prescribe olanzapine 5 mg intramuscular now for acute distress and admit to the short stay unit overnight for observation and social work review the following morning without discharge planning until psychiatry review
options.rationale: Antipsychotics are not first line for distress in borderline personality disorder and add metabolic and sedation risk; hospitalisation is not the AU default. (Source: NHMRC: Borderline Personality Disorder Guideline)

options.text: Repair the wound with sutures under local anaesthetic then discharge with no further follow up planned and advise her to attend her scheduled routine dialectical behaviour therapy group session in 4 days time
options.rationale: Deep suture may not be necessary for a superficial dermal cut; discharging without contacting her existing team or safety planning misses the AU standard of care. (Source: NHMRC: Borderline Personality Disorder Guideline)

options.text: Dress the wound with steristrips, complete a collaborative safety plan and dialectical behaviour therapy skill review, contact her case manager and arrange next day dialectical behaviour therapy contact before discharge home
options.rationale: AU NHMRC borderline personality disorder guideline supports collaborative safety planning, brief validating intervention and continuity with existing dialectical behaviour therapy team rather than admission for chronic self injury without imminent suicide risk. (Source: NHMRC: Borderline Personality Disorder Guideline)

options.text: Refer to community forensic mental health service because the pattern of repeated superficial self injury after interpersonal conflict now meets criteria for a formal risk assessment under the state high risk offender framework today
options.rationale: Forensic services are for offending behaviour not for self injury; this pathway is inappropriate and does not meet clinical need. (Source: NHMRC: Borderline Personality Disorder Guideline)

explanation.summary: Chronic self injury in borderline personality disorder is best managed with continuity of a structured psychological therapy such as dialectical behaviour therapy, mentalisation based treatment or schema therapy rather than repeated hospital admissions which are associated with dependency and iatrogenic worsening. Emergency department presentations should focus on wound care, brief validating intervention, collaborative safety planning, review of coping skills already learned in therapy, and rapid handover back to the treating team. Admission is reserved for acute suicidality with clear intent and plan, or for medical severity of the self injury. Pharmacotherapy has a limited role in borderline personality disorder; short courses of medication may be trialled for comorbid conditions but should not be started routinely for distress in the emergency department. Contacting the existing therapist and case manager the same day is central to the standard of care.
key_points: Chronic self injury in BPD without imminent suicide risk does not require admission.
Collaborative safety planning, wound care and rapid case manager handover is the AU standard.
Pharmacotherapy has a limited role in BPD; do not start antipsychotics or benzodiazepines routinely in the emergency department.
explanation.pearls: Collaborative safety planning and next day dialectical behaviour therapy contact is preferred over admission for chronic self injury in borderline personality disorder without imminent suicide risk under AU NHMRC guidance.

subtopic_detail: Recognition and lorazepam challenge in a young woman with new onset catatonia superimposed on major depressive disorder
stem:
You are the consultation liaison psychiatry registrar reviewing a 24 year old woman on the medical ward. She has a 3 year history of recurrent major depressive disorder currently on sertraline 100 mg daily but was admitted 24 hours ago with reduced oral intake and immobility for the past 5 days. Her Bush Francis catatonia rating scale confirms mutism, waxy flexibility, negativism, staring, posturing and prolonged immobility.

She has no fever (temperature 36.8 degC), heart rate 92 per minute, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, oxygen saturation 99 percent on room air. Creatine kinase is 380 U/L (30 to 200), sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.2, urea 5.6, creatinine 66 micromol/L, calcium and magnesium normal. Full blood count, C reactive protein and thyroid stimulating hormone are within normal limits. Neurological examination shows no focal deficit, no rigidity, no autonomic instability and no clonus. Computed tomography of the brain and cerebrospinal fluid examination are unremarkable. She has no known allergies and no recent antipsychotic use.

data_table.Vital signs: Heart rate 92 /min, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degC
data_table.Bush Francis: Mutism, waxy flexibility, negativism, staring, posturing, prolonged immobility
data_table.Bloods: Creatine kinase 380 U/L (30-200), sodium 138, potassium 4.2, calcium normal, TSH normal
data_table.Neurology: No focal deficit, no rigidity, no autonomic instability, no clonus; brain CT and CSF unremarkable

lead_in: What is the most appropriate diagnostic and initial management step?

options.text: Commence intramuscular haloperidol 5 mg for suspected acute psychotic episode with negative symptoms and observe for response over 4 hours before considering alternative sedative or benzodiazepine therapy
options.rationale: Antipsychotics can precipitate or worsen catatonia and risk neuroleptic malignant syndrome; they are contraindicated as first line in catatonia. (Source: RANZCP: Catatonia)

options.text: Arrange urgent electroconvulsive therapy under general anaesthesia today without a preceding benzodiazepine trial because electroconvulsive therapy is the definitive treatment for all catatonic presentations at first review
options.rationale: Electroconvulsive therapy is very effective and is used first line in malignant catatonia or lorazepam failure, but a lorazepam challenge is the AU first step in non malignant catatonia. (Source: RANZCP: Catatonia)

options.text: Give intravenous flumazenil 0.2 mg to reverse suspected benzodiazepine intoxication as the initial diagnostic and therapeutic manoeuvre before any additional psychiatric or neurological investigation is arranged
options.rationale: There is no history of benzodiazepine use and flumazenil has no role in catatonia; it may precipitate seizures if the patient is on benzodiazepines. (Source: RANZCP: Catatonia)

options.text: Commence intravenous 5 percent glucose infusion with intravenous thiamine 500 mg three times daily for suspected Wernicke encephalopathy without any additional psychiatric assessment or treatment on the medical ward
options.rationale: Wernicke would typically show ophthalmoplegia, ataxia and confusion; catatonic features are not primary and glucose without thiamine can precipitate Wernicke. (Source: RANZCP: Catatonia)

options.text: Give intravenous lorazepam 2 mg as a diagnostic and therapeutic challenge and reassess the Bush Francis catatonia rating scale at 15 minutes; a partial response supports a scheduled lorazepam regimen
options.rationale: The lorazepam challenge (1 to 2 mg IV, reassess at 15 minutes) is both diagnostic and therapeutic in catatonia; a partial response supports scheduled 2 mg three times daily and further titration. (Source: RANZCP: Catatonia)

explanation.summary: Catatonia is a neuropsychiatric syndrome characterised by disturbances of movement, speech and behaviour that can complicate mood disorders, psychosis, autoimmune encephalitis, medical illness and drug reactions. Diagnosis uses the Bush Francis Catatonia Rating Scale (2 or more of 14 items including immobility, mutism, staring, posturing, waxy flexibility, negativism, mannerisms, echolalia, echopraxia). A lorazepam challenge (1 to 2 mg intravenously or intramuscularly, reassessed at 15 minutes) is both diagnostic and therapeutic; a partial response confirms the diagnosis and supports scheduled lorazepam 2 mg three times daily titrated to response (up to 24 mg per day). Electroconvulsive therapy is highly effective and is first line in malignant catatonia (with fever, autonomic instability, rigidity or rhabdomyolysis) or in benzodiazepine failure. Antipsychotics can precipitate or worsen catatonia and are avoided.
key_points: Bush Francis Catatonia Rating Scale: 2 or more of 14 items supports the diagnosis.
Lorazepam 1 to 2 mg intravenous challenge is both diagnostic and therapeutic; reassess at 15 minutes.
Electroconvulsive therapy first line in malignant catatonia or lorazepam failure; avoid antipsychotics.
explanation.pearls: The lorazepam challenge in catatonia (1 to 2 mg intravenously with reassessment at 15 minutes) is both diagnostic and therapeutic; partial response supports scheduled 2 mg three times daily with titration up to 24 mg per day before considering electroconvulsive therapy.
